q-106896:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =\lambda v \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 2k+1 & -k\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =2k[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 \\ k+1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2k \\ 2k\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2=2k, \\ k+1=2k\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $k$ in the first equation, we get

$$
2=2k\,⟹\,k=1.
$$

Now, substituting $k=1$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}k+1 & =2k \\ 1+1 & =2\cdot 1 \\ 2 & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a true statement.

Therefore, the solution of the system is $k=1.$

q-158440:
For a function $f(x)$ to be a valid probability density function on a set $S,$ it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- ${\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$

For the given function, the second condition states that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{{x}^{3}}{k}\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

Computing the integral on the left-hand side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{{x}^{3}}{k}\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4k}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{16}{4k}-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{4}{k}=1\,⟹\,k=4.
$$

q-129389:
Recall that for any random variable $X$ and constant $a,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[aX]={a}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X].
$$

In our case, $a=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}X] & ={(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \text{Var}[X].\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the variance of $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

Additionally, we're given that $\text{E}[X]=-\frac{1}{2}.$ 

We start by computing $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & =(-2)^{2}\cdot f(-2)+(-1)^{2}\cdot f(-1)+{1}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{2}^{2}\cdot f(2) \\  & =4(\frac{1}{2})+1(\frac{1}{8})+1(\frac{1}{8})+4(\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{13}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{13}{4}-{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{13}{4}-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}X] & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 3 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

q-129399:
Recall that for any random variable $X$ and constants $a$ and $b,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[aX+b]={a}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X].
$$

In our case, $a=-4$ and $b=\sqrt{5}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\sqrt{5}-4X] & ={(-4)}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =16\cdot \text{Var}[X].\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the variance of $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

Additionally, we're given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{3}{4}.$ 

We start by computing $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={0}^{2}\cdot f(0)+{1}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{2}^{2}\cdot f(2) \\  & =0(\frac{3}{8})+1(\frac{1}{2})+4(\frac{1}{8}) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =1-{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\sqrt{5}-4X] & =16\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =16\cdot \frac{7}{16} \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{\infty }\frac{5}{{x}^{2}}\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{3}^{a}\frac{5}{{x}^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{3}^{a}5{x}^{-2}\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[(-5{x}^{-1})]}_{3}^{a} \\  & =-5\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{x}]}_{3}^{a} \\  & =-5\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =-5\cdot (0-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-152754:
We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}\,\text{d}t & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{2}^{a}\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{2}^{a}{t}^{-3/2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-2{t}^{-1/2}]}_{2}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}]}_{2}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(\frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(0-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-20869:
First, we substitute $u=2+{x}^{4}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4{x}^{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=4{x}^{3}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to -\infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=2+{x}^{4}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $-\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $2$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{4{x}^{3}}{{(2+{x}^{4})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\infty }^{2}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-{\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{4{x}^{3}}{{(2+{x}^{4})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{2}^{a}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{u}]}_{2}^{a} \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to \infty }(-\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-101736:
Let's work out each integral.

For the first integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(u-1)^{3}}\,\text{d}u & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{2}^{a}\frac{1}{(u-1)^{3}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{2(u-1)^{2}}]}_{2}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(-\frac{1}{2(a-1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{2(2-1)^{2}}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2(a-1)^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral is convergent.

For the second integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{1}3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{1}3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[{z}^{3}]}_{a}^{1} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1-{a}^{3}) \\  & =\infty ,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral diverges.

For the third integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-2}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-2}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[-\frac{1}{x}]}_{a}^{-2} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral is convergent.

In conclusion, only integral II is divergent.

q-6034:
We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{6}^{\infty }\frac{\text{d}z}{z} & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{6}^{a}\frac{\text{d}z}{z} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\operatorname{ln}⁡z]}_{6}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡a-\operatorname{ln}⁡6) \\  & =\infty -\operatorname{ln}⁡6 \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the integral is divergent.

q-76910:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4-\sqrt{3}{t}^{2}}{\sqrt{2}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+5)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\sqrt{6}t,\,3{t}^{2},\,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-\sqrt{6}t)}^{2}+{(3{t}^{2})}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{6{t}^{2}+9{t}^{4}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{(1+3{t}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =1+3{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{5}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}(1+3{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =(t+{t}^{3}){|}_{0}^{5} \\  & =5+125-0 \\  & =130.\end{aligned}
$$

q-127573:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & ={e}^{t}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =|{e}^{t}|\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & ={e}^{t}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & ={e}^{t}\sqrt{2({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{2}{e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{e}^{t}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /2}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

q-81678:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2-3{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =2t-{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =2(1)-(1)^{3}+C \\ 4 & =2-1+C \\ C & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=3+2t-{t}^{3}.$
